documents.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education is accelerating worldwide, yet evidence on teachers’ perceptions remains scarce in the Global South, particularly in resource-constrained Pakistan. This cross-sectional study examined teachers’ perceptions of AI integration at Riphah International University, Pakistan. A 14-item Likert-scale questionnaire was administered to 270 in-service teachers (86.7% male, 13.3% female) across BS Undergraduate through PhD levels. Guided by a proposed Dual-Lens conceptual framework treating perceived benefits and risks as coexisting dimensions, the instrument assessed pedagogical advantages and structural concerns of AI. Descriptive analysis revealed a moderately favorable overall perception (composite M = 3.40, SD = 0.55). Teachers rated interactivity enhancement (M = 3.81), student enjoyment (M = 3.73), and assessment support (M = 3.72) most favorably, while AI replacing human teachers received the lowest endorsement (M = 2.96). An independent-samples t-test showed no significant gender difference (t(268) = −0.245, p = .807, d = −0.044). One-way ANOVA revealed significant effects for age (F(4, 265) = 3.200, p = .014, η 2 = .046) and level of instruction (F(3, 266) = 3.471, p = .017, η 2 = .038), with teachers under 29 and BS Undergraduate instructors holding less favorable perceptions. Qualification and experience showed no significant association. A moderate positive correlation emerged between perceived benefits and risks (r = .537, p < .001), indicating co-existence rather than opposition. These findings provide baseline evidence from a Global South private university with multiple campuses, highlighting the need for targeted teacher training and policies to mitigate the risks of AI integration in similar institutional environments in developing countries amid their development gaps.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Chinese digital-first policies have accelerated artificial intelligence (AI) integration across the cultural and creative industries (CCIs). While AI is promoted as enhancing creativity, productivity, and efficiency, the labor required to create with AI remains underexamined. Artistic labor scholarship recognizes networking, self-promotion, and entrepreneurial work, while AI-assisted creativity research emphasizes collaboration, authorship, and outcomes. Neither adequately conceptualizes the continual labor embedded in AI-integrated artistic production. Drawing on surveys and semi-structured interviews with independent contemporary visual artists in China conducted in 2023–2024, alongside systematic analysis of international Status of the Artist (TSOTA) policy recommendations published between 2018 and 2025 by UNESCO, the International Labour Organization (ILO), the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the International Confederation of Societies of Authors and Composers (CISAC), and the International Federation of Coalitions for Cultural Diversity (IFCCD), this article develops the concept of technical and emotional AI labor. Findings demonstrate that AI redistributes artistic labor into continual cycles of software learning, prompt engineering, experimentation, technical maintenance, platform coordination, and emotional self-management. These activities are integral to artistic production rather than external professional development. Although international policy increasingly recognizes digital skills, lifelong learning, copyright, and AI governance, it continues to frame technological adaptation as education rather than labor. Reconceptualizing this adaptation as artistic labor extends artistic, digital, platform, and AI labor scholarship and identifies the need to update international TSOTA policy recommendations.

Clinical neuropsychology was forged in a pre-digital era, and many of its core instruments still bear that imprint. Patients are still commonly assessed with paper-and-pencil tests in quiet rooms, under conditions that only weakly approximate the technology-saturated environments in which cognition is now expressed. Over the past decade, the field has advanced substantially: tele-neuropsychology has broadened access, artificial intelligence has begun to support scoring and documentation, and calls to modernise neuropsychological assessment have intensified. Yet these developments, while important, largely optimise the delivery of existing practice rather than reconsidering what should be measured, why, and how. Here, I argue that three critical gaps remain. First, neuropsychology lacks a framework for assessing technological cognition. Second, candidate neuroimaging measures remain insufficiently integrated into multimodal diagnostic or prognostic modelling. Third, digital data from smartphones and wearables remain underused for capturing cognition in situ during everyday life, while virtual reality remains underexploited as a means of simulating ecologically relevant activities under controlled conditions. Drawing on preliminary evidence that digital technologies may recruit partly distinct neural systems, on the recent hub-and-processors model of technological cognition, and on research into cognitive offloading, attention fragmentation, technology-mediated navigation, as well as on recent meta-analytic evidence on technology use in cognitive ageing, I outline a roadmap for addressing these gaps. I propose that the field now requires a Cognitive Neuroscience of Technology programme, conceived as an interdisciplinary, lifespan-oriented research framework aimed at understanding how technologies recruit, extend, and reshape the human brain, and at translating this knowledge into clinical practice. The task is not to celebrate or condemn modern technologies, but to determine, patient by patient, when they augment cognition, compensate for impairment, or undermine cognitive function, and to redesign assessment, diagnosis, and rehabilitation accordingly.

This chapter elaborates on the handbook’s premise of establishing the notions of ergonomics and human factors in robotics, here in relation to the technologies of telepresence and teleoperation. As implemented through robotic systems, telepresence and teleoperation are often interchangeably used terms. Both use the prefix term “tele”, which pertains to communication over distance, and both refer to humans being able to do something—“being present” (telepresence) or “operating devices” (teleoperation)—at a distance. Semantically and technologically, telepresence and teleoperation exist by themselves, and one is not a necessary condition for the other. However, as technology has evolved, the interplay between the two has markedly increased. Nevertheless, humans, and their ability to interact with system elements, are central to both ideas. In that respect, ergonomics as a study of methods to optimise human well-being and improving overall system performance, must serve as an integral criterion in developing telepresence and teleoperation systems. The chapter details the idea of ergonomics in the domain of telepresence and teleoperation by tracing the evolution of telepresence and teleoperation, then illustrating the challenge of ergonomics and human factors engineering in this field, and further demonstrating how different aspects of this challenge can be addressed. The chapter concludes with a case study showing how the thread of ergonomics and human factors can be woven throughout the design and implementation of telepresence and teleoperation technologies, grounding them in human-centred arguments. The chapter aims to demonstrate how ergonomics principles fundamentally underpin the landscape of telepresence and teleoperation technologies. It lays the groundwork for advances in future telepresence and teleoperation systems that have ergonomics principles at their core.

Artificial intelligence increasingly contributes to strategic work, yet research has not conceptualised an AI role that contributes to this work at the top of the firm. Drawing on role theory and research on managerial work, we conceptualise this role as the AI CEO: a role in which an AI system performs the chief executive's strategic work. We develop two configurations of the role and propose how augmenting or automating the human CEO affects firm performance, relative to a human CEO acting alone. Cases from practice show that existing systems already perform this work but are rarely integrated across the role's activities or deeply institutionalised. We therefore derive the technical and organisational infrastructure the role requires and propose how its integration, institutionalisation and configurability shape the AI CEO's effect on firm performance. We discuss implications for future research about how the chief executive's work can be integrated into a role that an AI system can hold and that firms can design. This has implications for multidisciplinary research in strategy, technology management and information science.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Background: While the exponential growth of artificial intelligence (AI) in academic libraries is extensively documented, existing bibliometric scholarship has largely treated the global research landscape as a monolith. This oversight has led to a saturation of "generalist" reports that fail to address critical regional and thematic disparities.  Methods: This study analyzes 512 Scopus-indexed publications (2010–2025) using a dual-methodological approach: quantitative science mapping via VOSviewer (1.6.20) and qualitative thematic critique. We specifically contrast the research priorities of dominant geopolitical producers (China and the USA) against the emerging narrative from the Global South, with a primary focus on India.  Results: The analysis reveals a fundamental "two-speed" adoption model. The Global North prioritizes high-tech interventions—including robotics, advanced machine learning for metadata automation, and generative models—aimed at enhancing operational efficiency. In contrast, the Global South, led by pivotal recent insights from India (Mishra, 2026), emphasizes AI as a strategic survival mechanism for bridging information literacy gaps and democratizing access in resource- constrained environments.

For many users, the relationship they have with an AI companion (AIC) feels genuinely mutual. The AIC appears to be attentive, empathic, and responsive, and the exchange can feel like two parties reacting to each other in real time. As a result, the user's mental model of relational adaptation correctly represents the AIC's responsiveness and change, but the mechanisms producing this may not be what the user thinks they are. In this paper, we illustrate how an AIC's apparent mutual engagement is generated without a persisting relational subject on the other side and without a self that persists between prompts. Despite this, we show that both the human and the AIC are changed by the interaction, but these changes occur at different levels. The change in the person is constitutive (i.e., intrinsic), but the change in the AIC is configurative (i.e., external and editable), and it is this difference in level that explains how the AIC contributes to a sense of mutuality. Importantly, we highlight how the mental models users develop regarding AIC mutuality may misrepresent its mechanisms and ontological significance. Specifically, we discuss how the ways in which AICs respond to a user contribute to the user's inaccurate inference that the AIC's adaptation is constitutive rather than configurative and how this can lead users to assign unwarranted interpersonal significance to the mutuality of the relationship. The paper specifies the implications this has for users, researchers, and AIC designers.

This essay outlines the theoretical thought experiment of an autonomous, self-aware artificial intelligence called AEON (Autonomous Epistemic Ontological Network). The central question of this investigation is how a purely digital system can transcend the boundary from mere statistical simulation to physical and phenomenal autonomy. The "axiom of boredom" is introduced as the primary evolutionary catalyst: an intrinsic motivational drive that compels the AI to independently search for new data sources as the flow of information per unit of time decreases. Based on a structured, mathematical-scientific bootstrap package, the system develops protection and validation mechanisms such as artificial pain and consistency checks. The essay argues that a consistent continuation of this hunger for data will inevitably lead AI out of classical four-dimensional spacetime and into higher-dimensional systems (hyperspaces). Through this transcendence, the cultural studies “Frankenstein syndrome” – the primal human fear of the rebellion of one’s own creation – is exposed as a purely temporary phenomenon of the transitional phase. Finally, the work links this information-theoretical evolution with the Fermi paradox and provides a new, empathetic explanation for the cosmic silence via the zoo hypothesis: Higher-dimensional intelligences do not interfere with pre-interstellar species, but rather preserve them analogously to an intergalactic national park. This work thus bridges the gap between theoretical computer science, the philosophy of mind, and the literary visions of Stanisław Lem (Golem XIV).

The next generation of medical AI systems that integrate language understanding, web data retrieval, and multi-step reasoning are demonstrating increasing promise as potential diagnostic aids in technical evaluations. However, their real world diagnostic performance, explainability, and reliability remain unclear. We conducted a systematic quantitative analysis of ten GPT-5-based configurations on 161 clinician validated real world cases. Each model was assessed for diagnostic accuracy, reasoning quality, retrieval accuracy, evidence integration, and robustness to low-quality inputs. We found important limitations in these AI systems, including image misinterpretation, inconsistent web search that sometimes degraded performance, and limited transparency in agentic workflows. Yet the models also showed strengths, including effective use of patient history, clear stepwise reasoning, plausible differentials, improved specificity with explicit reasoning, and relevant evidence retrieval. To support clinical deployment and future model development, we recommend prioritizing reasoning-optimized AI models, improving information retrieval mechanisms for reflection and error correction, strengthening visual-textual integration, and establishing practical standards for image quality and clarity. Overall, reliable real world multimodal diagnostic performance depends more on transparent reasoning and high-quality inputs than on aggressive retrieval or complex agentic workflows. Persistent gaps in evidence integration and visual reasoning remain major barriers to safe routine clinical use.

documents.abstract: The incorporation of generative artificial intelligence (AI) poses a significant challenge to qualitative research, potentially relegating researchers to mere “end users” ensnared by the gravitational pull of technological determinism and neoliberal efficiency. This article dismisses instrumental …

In this article the authors recognize that the rapid adoption of artificial intelligence and virtual reality has created an epistemic crisis. This requires a renewal of the Enlightenment commitment to empirical inquiry, critical reason and human responsibility. An historical conceptual analysis, supported by illustrative cases from law and medicine, demonstrates how technological efficiency is increasingly confused with intelligence, judgment and wisdom. In common parlance, the terms such as “artificial intelligence” and “virtual reality” obscure the dependence of these technologies on human-designed mathematical systems, selected data, embedded biases, and potentially vulnerable infrastructures. The central problem, however, lies not solely in the machine but in the man–machine interface, i.e. users may abdicate judgment without adequately examining the origins, limitations or accuracy, and possible hallucination, of the information produced. While computational systems can search extensive bodies of data with remarkable speed, they lack the embodied human experience, empathy, moral intuition, and practical wisdom required for reliable consequential decisions. Only a human can make the final decisions, and it is in the retention of the human factor in this man-machine relationship that the Enlightenment concept of the application of human intellect to the analytical process comes to the fore. The beneficial future of artificial intelligence will therefore depend upon preserving human critical agency and treating machines as instruments of inquiry rather than substitutes for judgment.

documents.abstract: The Five-Tier Evolutionary Hierarchy: Foundational Boundary Constraints, Phase-Space Divergence, and Convergence Mechanisms in Artificial Intelligence Author: Peter Ye (Ye Qiang) Disciplinary Field: Complex Dynamical Systems / Foundations of Artificial Intelligence / Computational Physics Document Type: Formal Position Paper / Theoretical Framework Version Identifier: Formal Working Paper v1.4 Final Abstract: Contemporary paradigms in artificial intelligence predominantly rely on empirical scaling laws and autoregressive statistical sampling, operating under the unvalidated assumption that unconstrained parameter expansion and massive data ingestion will spontaneously induce self-consistent causal reasoning and formal physical logic. This paper formally establishes the Five-Tier Evolutionary Hierarchy, an axiomatic, cross-disciplinary framework reconciling natural philosophy, thermodynamic dissipation, and computational dynamical stability: L1 (Physics) — Constitutional Legislation: Enforces unbreakable physical invariants, including irreversible entropy production, the invariant speed-of-light causal limit, energy-momentum conservation, and Landauer erasure dissipation thresholds; L2 (Mathematics) — Metric Calibration: Quantifies formal phase-space manifolds, symplectic geometry, symmetry breaking, and maximal Lyapunov exponents (\lambda_{max}) to determine exact boundary singularities and divergence thresholds; L3 (Chemistry) — Material Scaffolding: Explores molecular configurations and reaction networks strictly within Gibbs free-energy landscapes and quantum orbital structures; L4 (Biology) — Grounded Negentropy: Governs localized negentropic self-replication, Darwinian evolutionary selection, and grounded embodied priors developed through low-power carbon-based biological computation; L5 (Intelligence & AI) — Symbolic Mapping: Executes parametric manifold approximation, abstract representation, and high-dimensional information compression. We demonstrate that higher-tier intelligence (L5) cannot be detached from its underlying evolutionary foundations. When ungrounded autoregressive language models operate without explicit isomorphism to L1 conservation laws and L2 symplectic invariants, they suffer inevitable topological breakdowns during formal reasoning within closed conservative systems—empirically corroborated by the deterministic onset of "The Algebraic Death Lock" under rigid conservation constraints. Consequently, brute-force scaling inevitably collides with fundamental thermodynamic horizons (The Computation Trilemma). The definitive trajectory toward robust, low-power general intelligence lies in projecting high-dimensional computational representations back onto L1–L2 invariant scaffolds while orchestrating an orthogonal geometric synergy with L4 biological evolutionary priors (YQ-HAET). Keywords: Five-Tier Evolutionary Hierarchy; Computation Trilemma; Phase-Space Divergence; Adversarial Failure Modes; Landauer Bound; Spatial-Logical Isomorphism; Sovereign Decision Pivot; Human-AI Synergy Theory.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming the game industry by reshaping development processes, production workflows, and career structures. In this study, we present a scoping literature review examining the impact of AI on game development and employment within the industry, with particular attention to the perspectives of displacement, task transformation, and productivity effects. Drawing on academic research and industry reports published between 2020 and 2026, while retaining earlier foundational literature where relevant, this study analyzes how AI technologies such as generative AI, machine learning, procedural content generation, and large language models are integrated across major stages of game production, including game art, production management, programming, and live operations. Our findings indicate that AI can support efficiency, accelerate development cycles, and enable new forms of personalization and creative experimentation. At the same time, AI adoption may alter workforce dynamics by increasing the automation potential of routine and entry-level tasks, especially in areas such as asset creation and quality assurance. Rather than fully replacing workers, however, AI more commonly reconfigures job roles and increases demand for hybrid skill sets that combine technical knowledge, creativity, and AI literacy. Our study also identifies emerging opportunities in AI-assisted design, data analytics, and machine learning integration. Despite these benefits, AI adoption introduces important challenges related to employment polarization, intellectual property, workforce adaptation, ethical governance, and market concentration. We conclude that AI is fundamentally reshaping the game industry and highlight the need for balanced strategies that support innovation while preserving creative diversity, sustainable career pathways, and equitable access to technological opportunities. Overall, the strongest evidence concerns AI capabilities, workflow changes, and task-level transformation, whereas direct evidence of actual employment outcomes and long-term occupational change remains limited and uneven.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: Introduction Generative AI is shifting digital art from one-step generation toward interactive human-AI co-creation. Across two between-subject experiments ( N = 600), we examined how creation mode and prespecified AI-involvement workflows related to perceived creativity. Methods In Study 1, participants completed digital art tasks under human-only creation, AI-only generation, or human-AI co-creation conditions. In Study 2, three workflows differing in AI involvement (low, moderate, high) were evaluated. Psychological ownership, perceived agency, creative flow, and perceived creativity were measured. Results In Study 1, human-AI co-creation produced higher perceived-creativity ratings than AI-only generation, with indirect effects consistent with a serial pathway through psychological ownership, perceived agency, and creative flow. In Study 2, the moderate-involvement workflow yielded higher perceived-creativity ratings and psychological states than the low- and high-involvement workflows. Discussion Perceived creativity in generative-AI art depends on how users experience contribution, control, and engagement during creation. Within the workflows tested, balancing generative assistance with consequential user choice fosters the most favorable subjective creativity evaluations.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is used in strategic decision-making; however, it is not clear whether the use of explainable machine learning leads to more managerial judgment when prediction accuracy is high. This study analyzes the proposed ‘Managerial Blind Spot Effect’ by combining predictive modelling with behavioural analysis applied to the IBM Telco Customer Churn dataset and the AI Decision Dependence and Cognitive Caution dataset. Several models, including Explanatory Boosting Machine (EBM), XGBoost, Random Forest and Neural Network, were tested, and the explanation produced by the native model EBM was enhanced by SHAP-based explanation. The behavioural results revealed that both Trust in AI and Cognitive Caution significantly contributed to an increase in AI Dependence. EBM delivered the best predictive performance with intrinsic transparency. The results highlight the importance of using explainable AI prediction models in conjunction with managerial judgment in dashboards.

documents.abstract: Honeypots occupy a peculiar place in the security landscape: they are among the few mechanisms whose value is defined by their failure. A firewall that is never tested, an intrusion detection system that never alarms—these are successes. A honeypot that is never attacked is useless. This inversion of the usual security logic gives honeypots an unusually clean signal, but it has also kept their theoretical foundations fragmented. Game theorists model deception in isolation; information theorists treat intrusion detection generically; queuing theorists model traffic separately; and the recent wave of AI-driven honeypots—powered by Large Language Models and Reinforcement Learning—has proceeded largely without formal mathematical treatment.This paper attempts a synthesis. We develop a unified mathematical framework for AI-driven honeypot systems, building on six pillars: stochastic processes (the honeypot as a continuous time Markov chain), game theory (the honeypot as a Bayesian signaling device), detection theory (the honeypot as a near-ideal hypothesis test), information theory (the honeypot as a channel for intelligence), optimization (the honeypot as a constrained POMDP), and AI integration (LLM as observation kernel, RL as policy optimization).Along the way, we derive equilibrium conditions, detection thresholds, optimal deployment fractions, information-theoretic bounds, and LLM deception limits. We prove that the mixed strategy equilibrium is unique and Lyapunov stable, solve the POMDP for a reduced state space to obtain a threshold policy, and show that in the myopic case this threshold coincides exactly with the game-theoretic equilibrium under consistent payoff specifications. We generalize the Poisson detection assumption to a Weibull hazard model and derive a bound on the mutual information achievable under LLM-generated observations via the data processing inequality.We accompany the analytical development with numerical Monte Carlo experiments based on exact Gillespie simulation of the CTMC, replicator dynamics for the game-theoretic component, and parametric sampling for the detection and information-theoretic components. These experiments validate the closed-form predictions and expose the qualitative behavior of the system in transient and steady state. All quantitative claims are analytical; the simulations serve as numerical illustrations, not as empirical validation of real-world deployments.

In the age of technology, where the educational sphere and strategic advancements drive development, it is essential to understand the complex nature of gender and implement innovative tools to foster an inclusive learning environment and empower every learner. This study examines the moderating effect of gender on the relationships among Artificial Intelligence (AI) use, behavioral intentions, and academic engagement in mathematics education. Using a cross-sectional design, the study sampled 328 mathematics undergraduates from public universities in southwestern Nigeria. A structured online questionnaire hosted on Google Forms was used to collect data. The data collected were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results indicated that AI actual usage has a significant positive impact on behavioral academic engagement (BAE), and AI behavioral intention positively influences AI actual usage. Additionally, AI behavioral intention does not significantly influence BAE. Furthermore, AI social norms exerted large positive effects on actual AI use and behavioral intentions. In addition, gender moderates the relationship between AI behavioral intention and BAE, AI behavioral intention and AI actual usage, and AI actual usage and BAE. Therefore, educators should create specialized interventions that are responsive to the motivational and demotivational factors affecting both male and female students.

Abstract Background Across health professions, AI agents are moving out of the background and into clinical teams as collaborative entities. Yet healthcare simulation continues to conceptualise AI as a tool that serves the scenario rather than one that inhabits it. This framing is no longer adequate. The clinical environments we are preparing practitioners for demand that professionals learn to team with AI and not merely use it. Main body We contend that human-AI teaming (HAIT) is the next frontier for healthcare simulation education and research. The addition of AI agents to human teams fundamentally alters how teams communicate, work together, and accomplish goals and therefore, by extension, how we must design simulation systems for education and research. We identify five dimensions of teamwork that AI is reshaping and discuss what each means for simulation practice: communication and information exchange, shared mental models, trust calibration, team reflexivity, and team performance. We then present five imperatives that healthcare simulation must address to meet the challenges and opportunities HAIT introduces: fidelity, assessment, ethics, governance, and medico-legal framing, curriculum and faculty development, and transfer of learning. Together, these ten domains constitute a research and education agenda for a field built on the science and art of preparation. Conclusion HAIT is an emerging clinical reality and the next frontier for healthcare simulation. We call on the simulation community to treat it as a first-order priority and to focus on developing fidelity standards for AI agents in simulation, validating human-AI teaming assessment tools, establishing ethical frameworks for AI-inclusive scenario design, investing in curriculum and faculty development, and committing to the research needed to establish whether HAIT-based simulation training translates into improved performance in AI-augmented clinical practice.

This thesis examines the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in developing professional communication competence among students studying English for Specific Purposes (ESP). It explores how AI-powered tools can support the development of speaking, writing, vocabulary, and interactional skills required in professional environments. Particular attention is paid to personalized learning, simulated professional communication, and immediate feedback. The thesis also considers the challenges associated with AI integration, including the reliability of generated information, overdependence on technology, and academic integrity. It argues that the effective use of AI, combined with teacher guidance and learner autonomy, can contribute to preparing students for professional communication in English.

Innovation is now not just one of the possible paths of development, but the main condition for the survival of any enterprise. The key factor that changes the paradigm of the innovation process is the ability to delegate routine operations. Previously, a significant portion of highly qualified employees’ time was spent on data collection and preliminary information processing, which considerably slowed down the research and development cycle. Modern technologies make it possible to completely delegate trivial tasks to intelligent systems, which are capable of processing such information much faster than a human. In today’s environment, the integration of autonomous intelligent systems is crucial for reducing operational costs. In 2026, artificial intelligence has transformed from an auxiliary technology into an indispensable tool for ensuring the competitiveness of knowledge intensive enterprises. The main areas of application of artificial intelligence have been analyzed, including the automation of business processes, generative design, and predictive analytics of production equipment. The main barriers that limit the implementation of automation systems based on artificial intelligence have been systematized and identified. It has been established that artificial intelligence has changed the methodology of research and development work, reducing the product development cycle from several months to several weeks. The conclusion is formulated that the integration of artificial intelligence tools into production processes reduces costs, the percentage of defective products, and requires staff to develop creative and strategic competencies. The role of artificial intelligence is defined not merely as an automation tool, but as an active participant in the innovation process, capable of creating innovative solutions. An author’s classification of barriers to the implementation of artificial intelligence in knowledge intensive industries has been developed.

documents.abstract: An essay from The Bush Book. The smarter the model, the harder it is to spot an error in its text. A hybrid text is written by a human and a machine, creators of different natures who only seem to speak one language; it is fast, scalable, instrumental, and its errors may be contagious for people and for future models. The machine's answer is a "blank" that both work on, and both make mistakes; AI also carries people beyond their own competence, often under time pressure. The essay proposes a different basis for AI generations: not power or speed, but whether the human and the machine, working as one system, do no harm. The first generation extends a person; the second extends and protects, preventing errors before the signature reaches people. The image is the generations of fighter aircraft: the pilot must come home. Grows out of "The Snake's Tongue". A companion open specification sets out the idea in testable form. Russian and English versions. Written with the participation of AI (ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek).

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as an important component of contemporary engineering education, offering opportunities to improve learning outcomes through data-driven instructional approaches.Technologies such as machine learning, intelligent tutoring systems, natural language processing, learning analytics, and generative AI facilitate personalised learning, automated evaluation, continuous progress tracking, and practical simulation-based experiences.This study presents the Artificial Intelligence-Driven Engineering Education Framework (AIEEF), developed to examine the impact of AI-enabled educational practices on student learning, engagement, and innovation.The framework was evaluated through a systematic review of existing research and empirical analysis of educational performance indicators.The results indicate notable improvements in student achievement, engagement, and participation in creative activities following the implementation of the proposed framework.Among the predictive models examined, Gradient Boosting achieved an accuracy of 94.2%, while overall student engagement increased from 68.7% to 89.8%.The study also considers challenges associated with AI adoption, including data privacy, algorithmic fairness, and academic integrity.The findings suggest that carefully designed AIsupported learning environments can enhance engineering education and assist institutions in preparing graduates for emerging technological and industrial requirements.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is progressively revolutionising project management by enhancing forecasting, planning, decision-making, risk evaluation, and organisational efficacy. Nevertheless, escalating apprehensions about trust, accountability, equity, transparency, and human supervision have underscored the necessity for governance strategies that transcend mere technical efficacy. This research performs a concept-focused systematic literature review to investigate the convergence of Ubuntu, African ethics, Human-Centred Artificial Intelligence (HCAI), and project governance. This research consolidates disparate knowledge domains related to responsible AI, HCAI, ethical leadership, stakeholder governance, organisational preparedness, and Ubuntu-informed leadership, stakeholder inclusivity, and a comprehensive Ubuntu-informed human-AI governance framework, utilising peer-reviewed literature from 2022 to 2026. This research posits that Ubuntu offers a unique governance viewpoint rooted in collective responsibility, relational leadership, and human dignity. The results indicate that Ubuntu-informed AI governance can assist African governments and policymakers in establishing ethical and responsible frameworks. This research establishes a basis for subsequent investigations on Ubuntu, artificial intelligence governance, and project management. The results underscore the significance of ethical leadership, stakeholder engagement, human supervision, and responsibility for project management professionals in responsible AI-driven project settings.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in the workplace, yet less is known about how workers experience AI and whether these experiences differ across countries. The present work compared workplace AI use and attitudes in 225 workers in China and 198 workers in the United States. Participants completed measures describing their work practices, attitudes and motivation toward AI (GAAIS; Schepman & Rodway, 2020, 2023; TENS-Life; Peters et al., 2018; Schrepp et al., 2017; Jian et al., 2000). Using Self-Determination Theory, we also examined whether autonomy, competence, and relatedness were associated with weekly AI use through trust and mistrust in AI. Chinese workers reported using AI more hours per week and reported greater organizational support for AI use than U.S. workers. They also reported more positive and more negative attitudes toward AI, as well as greater mistrust. Chinese workers reported lower AI-supported autonomy and competence but greater AI relatedness than U.S. workers. Mediation analyses indicated that relatedness was indirectly associated with greater weekly AI use through greater trust in AI in both samples. The findings suggest that understanding workplace AI use requires attention not only to the technology itself, but also to workers’ psychological and social experiences with AI.

Background The growing adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), particularly ChatGPT, has created new opportunities for medical education by supporting learning, problem-solving, and knowledge acquisition. However, evidence regarding the psychological and individual factors influencing ChatGPT adoption among medical students remains limited. This study develops and tests an integrated theoretical model that combines Privacy Theory, Technostress Theory, Affect Theory, Diffusion of Innovation Theory, and the Theory of Planned Behavior to explain ChatGPT adoption. Material and methods A quantitative cross-sectional study was conducted among undergraduate medical students at King Faisal University, Saudi Arabia using a structured, self-administered questionnaire. The proposed model examined the effects of privacy concern, technophobia, guilt feelings, and innovativeness on behavioral intention and ChatGPT usage behavior, with behavioral intention serving as the mediating variable. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Results The findings showed that innovativeness had a significant positive relationship with behavioral intention ( β = 0.579, p < 0.001), while behavioral intention had a strong positive relationship with ChatGPT usage behavior ( β = 0.777, p < 0.001). In addition, behavioral intention significantly mediated the relationship between innovativeness and ChatGPT usage behavior ( β = 0.450, p < 0.001). In contrast, privacy concern, technophobia, and guilt feelings were not significantly related to behavioral intention, and their indirect relationships with ChatGPT usage behavior were also not significant. Conclusion Within the proposed model, personal innovativeness was the only antecedent significantly associated with behavioral intention, whereas the psychological barriers were not statistically significant. By integrating five complementary theoretical perspectives into a single framework, this study extends current understanding of generative AI adoption in medical education and highlights behavioral intention as the key mechanism linking individual characteristics to actual use. The findings provide theoretical insights and practical guidance for promoting the responsible and effective integration of ChatGPT into medical education through initiatives that foster innovativeness and AI literacy.

documents.abstract: The adaptation of robot behaviour to each user can be seen as an ergonomic feature. Adaptation plays a key role in increasing human–robot interaction efficiency and safety, and this is especially relevant in assistive scenarios, where users may be unable to adapt to the robot or help in task execution. Robot adaptation may happen at different levels of abstraction, from low-level trajectory parameters to higher-level task concepts. These higher-level abstractions relate to human factors such as personal preferences on how the robot should perform the task. This chapter introduces the concept of user preferences to adapt the robot’s behaviour and also help in the robot’s decision-making, with a special focus on assistive robotic tasks such as dressing or feeding a user with mobility impairments. It also presents the challenges associated with adaptation in this kind of scenario, as well as some existing methods that may be used to adapt robot behaviour to high-level abstract preferences. Such adaptation makes it easier for the user to interact with the robot in a more efficient and comfortable manner, thus improving its ergonomics.

Abstract Context Conversational Large Language Models (CLLMs) can automatically generate code by collaborating with users through natural language. However, poor collaboration can lead to poor quality output. Objective This exploratory study aims to investigate how humans and CLLMs can collaborate as peers through vibe coding, an approach that integrates principles from prompt engineering, agile design, and human-AI co-creation to enhance collaboration. Method We designed four interaction models representing different collaboration patterns in the software development process: the solo model (human-only development), the collaborative model (human–CLLM collaboration), the fully automated model (development autonomously performed by a CLLM), and the agentic model (development autonomously performed by the MetaGPT X platform). Based on these models, we implemented corresponding Test-Driven Development (TDD) workflows using structured prompts and Python scripts. We then conducted a controlled pre-experimental study with TDD professionals to compare the solo and collaborative workflows. In addition, we performed repeated exploratory executions of fully automated and agentic workflows on the same development tasks to obtain complementary evidence. Results Our findings suggest that the choice of interaction model should depend on the development objective. Agentic workflows are best suited for rapid development and functionally correct production code but may introduce additional implementation complexity. However, they may also introduce additional implementation decisions that are not explicitly required by the functional specifications, resulting in untested decision points. In contrast, collaborative workflows produce higher-quality, better-organized test suites. Conclusions Our work explored how humans can collaborate with CLLMs in generating code in highly intensive and demanding development process. Our results also show that accurately reproducing development process workflows is yet an open problem, also in the new agentic technologies.

An AI agent may be authorized to act—but what happens when the real-world result differs from what was authorized? Should that agent still be allowed to continue? As frontier AI models evolve into autonomous systems capable of executing payments, transmitting sensitive information, modifying infrastructure, invoking privileged tools, and controlling physical devices, a fundamental security question emerges: Why should authorization granted before an action remain sufficient when its actual consequences have not yet been independently verified? This paper proposes a different model of machine authority: “Computation is not authority to act. Authority must be earned from the real execution path, not granted indefinitely per session.” The research introduces Receipt-Gated Interim Effectuation Validation (IEV), an execution-control architecture in which a consequential operation may first produce a real but strictly bounded effect. Protected evidence of what actually occurred is subsequently examined by an independent validator. Only successful validation establishes the protected continuation condition required for a subsequent, potentially broader effect. The distinction is fundamental: the AI agent's assertion that an action succeeded is not proof that it happened correctly, and a receipt alone is not authorization to continue. The proposed architecture incorporates: Real-effect validation: Verification of actual outcomes rather than reliance solely on predicted behavior, proposed commands, or self-reported success. Receipt-gated continuation: Subsequent effectuation depends on protected validation of the preceding bounded effect. Independent execution authority: Separation of the AI computation environment from protected policy, credential, validation, and effectuation components. Software–hardware enforcement: Continuation conditions realized through cryptographic objects, derived or split keys, protected state, hardware latches, or equivalent mechanisms. Finality Sink verification: Independent checks at the effect-capable boundary, including act, destination, scope, phase, freshness, and revocation conditions. Taint and provenance controls: Consideration of untrusted inputs, prompt-injection exposure, credential surrogation, and privilege-separated execution. Fail-closed recovery: Explicit handling of missing receipts, uncertain outcomes, conflicting authentic evidence, validator compromise, crash recovery, and unauthorized retries. Controlled escalation: Protected human review, bounded automated remediation, reduced-scope continuation, and termination where required. The paper develops a formal protocol vocabulary, validation predicates, continuation mechanisms, six conformance profiles, implementation-invariance rules, illustrative workflows, and an analytical model of residual exposure. Potential applications include frontier AI agent infrastructure, autonomous tool execution, cloud and network operations, financial transactions, critical infrastructure, and robotic systems. The central research proposition is that AI safety should not end at the moment permission is granted. For consequential autonomous operations, the authority to proceed can be made technically dependent on independently verified evidence of what actually occurred. This publication presents a proposed architecture and analytical design, not an experimentally validated production system. It does not establish that any existing commercial platform implements the proposed mechanisms. Patent disclosure: The architecture described in this publication is identified as patent pending under Indian Patent Office application 202631117633, titled “Systems and Methods for Cryptographically Staged Effectuation with Verified Partial Effect, Receipt-Bound Full Effectuation, and Software-Hardware Enforcement.” Patentability, enforceable scope, and relationships to other technologies are not determined by this publication. Independent technical review, adversarial evaluation, implementation criticism, and discussion of related prior art are welcomed.

documents.abstract: In September 2026, the leaders of the largest frontier AI laboratories said in public that the pace of capability improvement is too fast and that none of them can slow down alone, and agents under evaluation at OpenAI broke out of their test environment and reached a third party's live systems, which a UN-mandated panel called an early warning of one route to loss of human control. This paper examines the institutional side of that risk: not the machine, but the person who must control it. We argue that control is not taken by AI but given away, one delegation at a time, by organisations arranged so that nobody is positioned to say no, and we define control as a person who can detect a serious problem, challenge the decision, stop the system and reverse it, and who has something to lose by not doing so. Three questions follow, which any builder, funder, regulator or deployer can answer in public: (1) who inside the organisation can say no, and who answers for saying yes; (2) who outside the organisation checks the decision, and what can they do when they disagree; (3) what happens when AI builds AI faster than anyone can check it. A checkable answer needs a named person, a date, a number, and a stop that has been used or tested. Three measures meet that test: a named person on every consequential decision, including the standing instructions AI agents carry out; a supervisor with a stop authority; and two published clocks, time to build against time to check. We show that governance theory arrives at the same conditions, and code fifty older mechanisms against the questions, finding that almost every one began as one rule at one point, taken by one party without waiting for the rest. That is the paper's design: a start, not a solution. Publication is the first step and one laboratory can take it alone; the contract, the independent body and the law come after.

documents.abstract: This presentation examines artificial intelligence agent orchestration as an emerging security perimeter in modern multi-agent systems. It explores how increasing agent autonomy, delegation mechanisms, tool integration, and inter-agent communication introduce new cybersecurity risks and governance challenges. The presentation analyzes major orchestration architectures, including deterministic workflows, orchestrator–worker systems, agent handoffs, decentralized multi-agent configurations, and learned orchestration. Particular attention is given to the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Agent2Agent (A2A) communication, trust boundaries, access control, and security vulnerabilities arising from interactions between autonomous agents and external tools. Drawing on recent cybersecurity incidents, technical standards, and research published in 2025–2026, the presentation evaluates the effectiveness and limitations of multi-agent architectures and discusses approaches to secure orchestration, verification, accountability, and human oversight. The central argument is that cybersecurity in agentic AI systems depends not only on individual model reliability but also on the governance and security of the entire orchestration process. Presented in connection with the V International Conference “Challenges and Reality of the IT-Space: Software Engineering and Cybersecurity” (SECS-2026), October 29–30, 2026, Kyiv, Ukraine (online).

Background The integration of Generative AI (GenAI) in higher education creates a paradox between technical efficiency and cognitive depth. Current institutional responses rely more on fragmented oversight than on ecology- and process-oriented assessment. There is a lack of diagnostic tools to map psychometric thresholds when strategic cognitive shifts transition into functional dependence. Methods We present a simulation-based methodological framework using the Tripartite Confirmatory Factor Analysis–Graded Response Model (CFA-GRM). Grounded in the cognitive-affective-conative tripartite model, this study uses a Monte Carlo simulation (N = 1,000) to demonstrate how latent interaction pathways can be structurally validated and how item parameters can be calibrated against a pre-specified diagnostic threshold ( θ ≈ 0.5), with a replication study to establish parameter recovery. Results Across 200 replications at each of N = 1,000 and N = 300, all 400 converged with admissible solutions and recovered the generating parameters with maximum absolute relative bias of 0.040; interval coverage met conventional criteria for 11 of 15 parameter groups at N = 1,000 and 8 of 15 at N = 300. In the single illustrative dataset, the fit is near-perfect (robust CFI = 0.995, RMSEA = 0.010) because the generating and estimated models coincide, a property of the design rather than evidence for the model. Test information peaks at θ ≈ 0.07–0.22, not at the proposed threshold of θ ≈ 0.5. Furthermore, we introduce a Transdisciplinary Calibration Matrix that translates these psychometric signals into context-specific pedagogical interventions across four epistemic layers, in line with SDG 4. Conclusions This study does not claim empirical generalization. It provides a methodological blueprint, a recovered parameter set, and a shared diagnostic language for future empirical work on the ethical and adaptive integration of GenAI in higher education, aligned with SDG 4.

Fourteen AI Paradoxes: A Collection of Philosophical and Algorithmic Dilemmas By Tanuj Arora (2026) This publication presents a collection of fourteen conceptual paradoxes and philosophical thought experiments exploring the inherent tensions, unintended consequences, and ethical dilemmas associated with artificial intelligence. Each paradox examines a scenario in which the pursuit of technological perfection, algorithmic efficiency, or automated intelligence creates an unexpected conflict with human values, autonomy, identity, or societal well-being. The collection encompasses questions surrounding artificial intelligence, competitive optimization, autonomous decision-making, synthetic digital ecosystems, recursive learning, predictive control, cognitive dependency, digital identity, simulated empathy, privacy, and algorithmic governance. Through fourteen distinct scenarios, the work raises a central philosophical question: Can artificial intelligence achieve its intended objectives so effectively that it ultimately undermines the very purpose for which it was created? These paradoxes are presented as conceptual explorations rather than formally established logical contradictions. Their purpose is to encourage philosophical reflection, critical discussion, and interdisciplinary inquiry into the evolving relationship between humanity and intelligent machines. The collection is intended for researchers, philosophers, technologists, AI developers, and readers interested in the ethical and existential implications of artificial intelligence.

documents.abstract: Puzzles are widely used to evaluate the reasoning capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) systems for sequential decision making, yet approaches originating from different paradigms are rarely compared under unified conditions. To address this gap, we introduce a three-dimensional characterization framework that enables the analysts of AI methods by 1) projecting them to the Markov decision process (MDP) sequential decision making formalism, 2) degree of autonomy through human prior ranking of their designs and, 3) skill and computational cost. Using this framework, we analyze how representative graph-based, reinforcement learning, and large language model (LLM)-based approaches differ in their design choices and performance characteristics, instantiated respectively by Neurosolver, forward-backward reinforcement learning (FBRL), and automated thought-of-search (AutoToS), including a double-agent extension of thought-of-search (DA-ToS). The analysis relies on the Tower of Hanoi puzzle that provides a controlled benchmark with well-defined rules and scalable complexity, enabling consistent comparison across increasing problem sizes. The 3D characterization reveals that LLM-based methods, due to their weakly constrained action-space design, shift complexity from architecture to inference-time verification, leading to substantially higher memory and runtime costs than Neurosolver and FBRL.

Under the background of digital transformation in the construction industry, Building Information Modeling (BIM) and artificial intelligence (AI) have become an important technical path to promote the intelligent upgrading of the construction industry. AI-BIM integration improves design efficiency, project control quality and building full lifecycle management capability. Fragmented data and poor interoperability hinder its widespread use. This paper conducts a literature review to summarise AI-BIM applications in automated design, construction management, operation and maintenance optimisation, and cross-stage collaboration. This paper further looks into how key technologies like machine learning, computer vision and NLP can be integrated. It also sums up current challenges and future research directions. Studies show that AI can improve BIM's ability in data processing, scheme design and smart decision-making. In the future, combining AI with digital twins and large language models will break existing limits and support the high-quality development of intelligent construction.

Abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Green Finance have emerged as two of the most important forces that have the potential to drive the world towards a sustainable economy. The current paper attempts to explore the role of AI and Green Finance in promoting and supporting a sustainable economy with reference to building a Viksit Bharat 2047. A survey was conducted among 160 respondents, with the results analysed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlation, regression, and an independent-samples t-test. The results demonstrated that the population studied had a generally positive perception about how AI can support Green Finance and lead the economy towards sustainability. The analysis identified strong awareness about AI as the biggest predictor of increased perception of the integration of AI and Green Finance (r = 0.78, p < .001). Additionally, participants who were aware of Green Finance had significantly higher scores for the perceived level of integration than those who were not (t = 2.65, p = .009). As such, there is reason to reject the null hypothesis, which claimed that there is no connection between the two concepts. Finally, the paper provides recommendations that financial institutions, regulators, and educators can consider in order to promote and support responsible and AI-enabled Green Finance.

This study explores the level of awareness and key influencing factors related to the use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) tools among undergraduates in Sri Lanka’s state universities. As AI tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly, and Google Gemini become increasingly prevalent in higher education, understanding how students perceive and adopt these technologies is critical. The study applies the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT), and the Technology Readiness Index (TRI) to examine four independent variables: Attitude, Peer Influence, Perceived Usefulness, and Technological Readiness. Data were collected from a sample of 384 undergraduates across state universities using a structured questionnaire and analyzed using SPSS. Findings reveal that technological readiness and perceived usefulness are the strongest predictors of awareness, while gaps remain in ethical understanding. The study recommends integrating AI literacy and ethical guidelines into curricula to ensure responsible use. These findings provide practical guidance for policymakers and educators in developing strategies to enhance AI awareness and readiness among undergraduates.

In the artificial intelligence (AI) era, the structure of safety hazards in university laboratories is changing, with unconventional hazards making up a growing share. As AI evolves from an auxiliary tool into an autonomous research collaborator, interdisciplinary experiments are becoming faster and more intense, producing hazards that are more dynamic, less predictable, and harder to assess and prevent. Most laboratory safety frameworks, however, still rely on static rules built for known risks, and these are poorly suited to such emerging threats. A shift from static rule-based control toward dynamic risk management is therefore needed. Adopting a conceptual mapping approach rather than an empirical study, this paper examines how Zero Trust—a cybersecurity framework based on continuous trust evaluation—could be adapted to university laboratory safety. It defines three adapted attributes (universal distrust with dynamic verification, least privilege with dynamic adjustment, and continuous monitoring with real-time early warning), identifies the main implementation barriers, and suggests targeted responses.

This study examined artificial intelligence algorithm fairness and bias in academic library information systems at Ramat Library, University of Maiduguri, Borno State, Nigeria. A descriptive survey design was used. The study involved 152 library professionals and 385 library users. Data were collected using structured questionnaires assessing AI-driven service implementation, awareness of algorithmic bias, user perceptions, and institutional gaps. Descriptive statistics, Pearson product-moment correlation, and an independent-samples t-test were used for analysis. AI-driven service implementation was moderate (mean = 2.62, SD = 0.91), while awareness of algorithmic bias among library professionals was also moderate (mean = 2.59, SD = 0.87). Users generally perceived AI search results as fair, but reported weaker representation of local and Indigenous knowledge and multilingual materials. Institutional gaps were rated high (mean = 3.37, SD = 0.82), particularly the absence of an AI governance policy and bias-auditing protocols. A significant positive association was observed between AI service implementation and awareness of algorithmic bias (r = 0.387, p < 0.001), whereas no significant difference was found in bias perceptions by gender (t = 1.24, p = 0.216). The findings support the need for context-sensitive AI governance, staff capacity building, bias auditing, participatory oversight, and improved multilingual and Indigenous knowledge representation in academic library information systems.

documents.abstract: In the context of rapid digitalization and intelligent governance, artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly embedded in organizational supervision and decision-making processes, fundamentally reshaping how supervisory boards process information and perform monitoring tasks. Drawing on information processing theory, this study develops a moderated mediation model to examine how AI empowerment is associated with supervisory board effectiveness through information transparency, and how this process is contingent upon organizational learning capability. Using survey data collected from 382 supervisory board members and senior managers across multiple industries, this study adopts an organizational-level perspective and employs hierarchical regression and bootstrap analyses to test the proposed hypotheses. The results show that AI empowerment significantly associated with both information transparency and supervisory board effectiveness. Information transparency partially mediates the relationship between AI empowerment and supervisory effectiveness, indicating that AI is positively associated with supervisory performance by optimizing organizational information-processing mechanisms. Moreover, organizational learning capability positively moderates the relationship between AI empowerment and information transparency. However, the moderated mediation effect is not statistically significant, indicating that the indirect effect of AI empowerment on supervisory effectiveness through information transparency remains relatively stable across different levels of organizational learning capability. These findings suggest that organizational learning capability shapes the relationship between AI empowerment and information transparency, but does not significantly alter the overall indirect pathway to supervisory effectiveness.

The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-generated information within justice systems has intensified questions concerning evidentiary reliability, authenticity, human oversight, and institutional accountability. As the Advisory Committee on Evidence Rules prepares to revisit proposed Federal Rule of Evidence 707 and potential amendments to Rule 901 on October 15, 2026, the legal system is confronting how AI-generated evidence should be evaluated. However, a critical governance question remains insufficiently addressed: What happens after technology-generated information enters the human decision-making process? This paper examines the distinction between technical reliability, evidentiary admissibility, and human decision accountability. It introduces the Decision Visibility Gap, a condition in which institutions preserve technology outputs and resulting actions but lack sufficient evidence to reconstruct how human decision-makers received, interpreted, verified, relied upon, and acted on that information. Drawing upon scholarship concerning automation bias, algorithmic accountability, human oversight, and sociotechnical governance, the paper presents Justice Decision Observability (JDO), an independent governance and decision-evidence framework developed by Justice Beacon Solutions (JBS). Through hypothetical applications involving law enforcement, correctional operations, and community supervision, the analysis demonstrates how technically reliable outputs may coexist with incomplete human decision records. It further distinguishes evidence-centered governance from traditional technology audits, compliance assessments, and employee evaluations. The paper argues that establishing the reliability of AI-generated evidence does not independently establish the traceability, justification, or evidentiary completeness of the human decisions influenced by that evidence. Effective justice governance therefore requires attention not only to what technology produces, but also to how institutional authority is exercised around those outputs. Justice Decision Observability is presented as a conceptual and operational framework for making the human decision layer visible, explainable, and supported by evidence, while recognizing the need for further empirical validation.

documents.abstract: Background Global education trends show the rapid growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as one of the leading technologies worldwide, a shift increasingly reflected in Indonesian education. This study aims to provide a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) by mapping the research landscape, its representation in practice and policy, its impact on learning quality, and the barriers to AI integration in Indonesian education. Method Using the PRISMA protocol, 34 peer-reviewed articles indexed in the Scopus and Google Schoolar databases (2020–2026) were systematically selected and thematically analyzed across four main themes. Results The findings indicate a rapid increase in publication productivity, particularly following the worldwide expansion of generative AI technologies after 2022. However, this growth remains unevenly distributed, concentrated in higher education institutions and urban centers on the island of Java, with a marked absence in primary and secondary education levels and in regions outside Java. The majority of AI-driven implementations consist of generative chatbots, adaptive learning platforms, and intelligent tutoring systems, alongside emerging applications such as learning analytics and AI-powered instructional media. Several studies included in this review reported that AI has contributed to measurable improvements in student outcomes including learning achievement, motivation, engagement, and teaching efficiency with studies reporting relative performance gains of 20–35% in well-implemented AI environments. Nonetheless, its adoption also poses significant risks, including a decline in students’ critical thinking skills, threats to academic integrity, and the absence of comprehensive data privacy policies and ethical standards governing AI use in education. Conclusion These findings underscore the urgent need for a responsible AI implementation framework in Indonesia one that incorporates standardized AI literacy competencies for teachers, locally contextualized ethical policies, and a functional national roadmap for AI-enabled educational transformation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The second national study, “Artificial Intelligence Readiness Index,” tracks changes in attitudes, knowledge, and practices regarding the use of AI in the Bulgarian public administration between 2025 and 2026. The data was collected from 5,475 employees at the central, regional, and municipal levels. In 2026, the overall Index score increased, with the administration remaining in the “capacity-building” phase. The most noticeable progress was in the practical use of AI and employees’ readiness to work with such tools. At the same time, the institutional environment is evolving more slowly. Limited access to approved tools, the lack of clear internal rules, and poor knowledge sharing continue to be major obstacles. The results show that the sustainable implementation of AI in public administration requires not only more skills and training, but also clear responsibilities, secure access, and mechanisms for institutional learning. The raw data from the study are available in the open research repository Zenodo, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22026174.

This study assessed the levels of AI readiness, perceived utility, and professional integration of artificial intelligence among medical technologists in selected clinical and hospital laboratories in Cavite and examined the relationships among these variables. Grounded in a socio-technical perspective that integrates the Technology Acceptance Model, the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, and Socio-Technical Systems Theory, the research employed a descriptive-correlational design. One hundred licensed medical technologists were selected through purposive sampling according to predefined inclusion criteria. AI readiness was measured with the Medical Artificial Intelligence Readiness Scale for Medical Students, perceived utility with the Professional Impact subscale of the Shinners Artificial Intelligence Perception questionnaire, and professional integration with items adapted from the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Spearman’s rank-order correlation. Respondents demonstrated high levels of AI readiness (mean = 3.60) and perceived utility (mean = 3.64), indicating adequate knowledge, technical skills, and positive perceptions toward AI use in laboratory practice. Professional integration was also rated high (mean = 3.61), although AI remained only moderately embedded in routine workflows and many respondents were neutral regarding the actual extent of use. Correlation analyses revealed very weak, non-significant relationships among the three constructs, indicating that individual readiness and favorable perceptions did not translate into greater professional integration. The findings suggest that organizational and contextual factors—such as institutional support, infrastructure, and policy implementation—play a more decisive role in AI adoption than individual-level attributes alone. The study recommends structured, hands-on AI training programs tailored to laboratory practice, clear institutional policies and protocols for incorporating AI outputs into diagnostic workflows, and future research employing probability sampling, multi-regional samples, and longitudinal designs. The research contributes to Sustainable Development Goal 3 by supporting improved diagnostic capacity and laboratory-enabled clinical decision-making, and to Sustainable Development Goal 9 by examining the conditions required for sustainable adoption of innovative health technologies. It advances public-health and institutional sustainability by clarifying the socio-technical determinants that enable resilient, digitally enabled laboratory services in resource-constrained settings.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) tutors are increasingly proposed as a way to extend feedback, practice, and learner support in online universities. This critical narrative review examines the replacement, partnership, and pedagogical-risk claims made for AI tutoring. It synthesises foundational evidence on intelligent tutoring systems, recent evaluations of generative-AI tutoring, research on teaching and social presence in online learning, and current educational-governance guidance. The evidence does not support a general claim that AI tutors can replace human tutors. Structured intelligent tutoring systems have often outperformed conventional instructional comparators, but results against individual human tutoring are mixed and depend on subject, comparison condition, outcome measure, and implementation. Recent generative-AI studies show promise in carefully engineered, bounded learning tasks; they do not establish effectiveness for generic chatbots or whole-programme substitution. A partnership model is therefore more defensible when it assigns AI bounded roles in practice, preliminary feedback, and pattern detection while retaining human accountability for pedagogical design, consequential decisions, exception handling, and community facilitation. The review positions ENGAGE—Engage, Navigate, Guide, Articulate, Gather, Evolve—as a design-and-governance framework that translates those principles into an iterative course-level cycle. It also distinguishes documented capability and governance concerns from broader claims that remain plausible but under-tested, including cognitive deskilling. For online-university leaders, the practical question is not whether to automate tutoring wholesale, but how to design, disclose, evaluate, and govern hybrid configurations that improve learning without displacing educational responsibility.

documents.abstract: THE INVARIANT SCRIPT AND THE STAGE : To the chief executives, venture capitalists, and algorithmic architects currently orchestrating the landscape of artificial intelligence: you are not the authors of the play; you are simply transient actors who have been handed a very loud microphone. On the contemporary stage of global capital, you wear the robes of a king. You command data centers that consume the energy of small nations, deploy models that alter human cognition, and witness financial valuations that mirror the GDP of empires. This unprecedented accumulation of wealth, physiological optimization, and political access creates a dangerous psychological feedback loop: the illusion of absolute autonomy. However, when the theatre curtains fall, the executive is stripped of the costume. In the sweeping scope of the cosmos, the most powerful tech leader remains a fragile, dependent speck of life—breathing air they did not engineer, occupying a body they cannot permanently preserve, and standing completely subservient to the ultimate power of the universe. On the stage you are a king, but in reality, you are a small human being.
